title: Customs Valuation Documentation for Motor Vehicles
summary: The concept evolved from a general requirement for manufacturer-issued invoices for customs valuation of motor vehicles into a structured, multi-tiered verification framework. It transitioned from a simple mandate to provide a manufacturer's invoice to a system that allows for certified invoices or, in their absence, the use of international market valuation benchmarks (Yellow Book, Glass's Guide).

evolution.valuation_methodology: Shifted from a singular reliance on manufacturer invoices to a flexible hierarchy including certified invoices and international price journals.
evolution.legal_structure: Moved from a broad mandate to a specific, clause-based procedural framework.

timeline.change: Established the initial requirement for manufacturer-issued invoices for customs valuation of motor vehicles.
Reiteration of the 2011 valuation requirement framework.
Formalized a three-tier valuation hierarchy: direct manufacturer invoice, certified invoice, or third-party market valuation benchmarks.

Customs Act 1969: The Government issued this S.R.O. under the authority granted by Section 25(3) of the Customs Act 1969 to determine the minimum value for customs duty assessment on specific motor vehicles.
The Act defines the framework within which the First Schedule is maintained and under which the Government may prescribe valuation criteria for imported goods.
S.R.O. 190-AIN/2010: This previous customs notification is explicitly repealed by the current S.R.O.
First Schedule: The First Schedule of the Customs Act 1969 identifies the specific H.S. Codes under Heading Numbers 87.03 and 87.04 that are subject to the new vehicle valuation requirements established by this order.
Customs Duty: This order establishes the criteria for determining the minimum value used to assess customs duty on the import of new motor cars, double cabin pick-ups, and other motor vehicles.
Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers are mandatorily required to submit an invoice issued directly by the manufacturer during customs clearance.
Price certificates or invoices issued by dealers or agents of the manufacturer are explicitly declared unacceptable for the purpose of establishing minimum value.
Value: The declared value in the manufacturer's invoice serves as the minimum value for assessment purposes, provided that higher values found in recognized international price guides or official manufacturer price lists take precedence if they exceed the invoice price.

Valuation for imports from Japan is referenced against the Yellow Book, while imports from other countries are referenced against the Glass's Guide or other reliable internationally recognized pricing publications.

Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: invoice issued directly by the manufacturer

Customs Valuation: This clause provides a hierarchy of valuation methods to be applied when the required invoice is not submitted during import clearance. The authorities may use the declared value of identical brand, model, and capacity vehicles imported by diplomats or privileged institutions as a valuation basis.
For vehicles manufactured in Japan, the average price of all code models quoted in the Yellow Book may be accepted for customs valuation purposes.

For vehicles imported from countries other than Japan, the average price of all code models as published in updated international trade journals like Glass's Guide or Magazine Automobiles may be utilized as the valuation basis.
Customs Act 1969: Section 81 of the Act authorizes the provisional assessment of goods where the declared value is adjusted by a minimum specified percentage if standard valuation criteria cannot be met.

This provision requires that following a provisional assessment, a mandatory post-clearance audit or investigation must be conducted to verify the value through manufacturer data or other reliable sources to finalize the customs assessment.
Customs Audit: The clause mandates that for provisionally assessed imports, a formal post-clearance audit or investigation is required to determine the final dutiable value based on verified data collected from manufacturers or other independent sources.

Customs Valuation: vehicles imported from countries other than Japan

Customs Act 1969: This SRO is issued under the authority of section 25(3) of the Customs Act 1969 to establish valuation conditions for motor vehicles.
It mandates the repeal of the previous notification S.R.O. 298-AIN/2011/2369/Customs.
First Schedule: The order applies to specific motor vehicles, double cabin pick-ups, and other vehicles classified under Heading 87.03 and 87.04 of the First Schedule.
Customs Duty: The order defines the procedure for determining the minimum value of imported new motor vehicles to ensure the proper assessment and collection of customs duty.
Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers must submit a manufacturer's invoice for the valuation of imported vehicles.
In cases where the importer is not the manufacturer, the invoice issued by the exporter must be certified by the manufacturer.
If a manufacturer directly issues invoices, invoices from third-party exporters will not be accepted for customs valuation purposes.

The manufacturer-certified invoice serves as the minimum value for assessment, though higher values found in recognized international publications or official price lists must be used if they exceed the invoice price.
The valuation of new vehicles must not be lower than the value of used, old, or reconditioned vehicles of the same brand, model, and cylinder capacity from the same country of origin.
S.R.O. 298-AIN/2011/2369/Customs: This notification is formally repealed by the current SRO.
